content.title: About
content.content: Soft frozen breadsticks are a ready‑to‑bake product made from wheat flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt. After freezing they retain shape and moisture, and when baked they become aromatic, golden‑brown and slightly crisp on the outside while staying soft inside.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen breadsticks can be stored up to 12 months without quality loss.
They are traditionally served alongside soups, salads or used as a base for appetizers.
Rapid flash‑freezing preserves the dough’s aroma compounds and texture.
In some countries they are called “soft pretzel sticks” and are popular street‑food items.
They can be flavored with herbs, cheese or garlic without affecting shelf life.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Breadsticks provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough supplies thiamine, niacin and riboflavin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked snacks, soft breadsticks are typically low in fat unless enriched with cheese or butter.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: They pair well with protein‑rich foods such as cheese, ham or hummus for a more balanced snack.

items.title: Fiber content (when whole‑grain)
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour adds dietary fiber, beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat flour and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapidly absorbed carbs can raise blood sugar, which diabetics should monitor.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties are heavily salted; those watching sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficiently baked sticks may remain cold inside, increasing the risk of bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the sticks at room temperature or in the refrigerator, then bake in a preheated oven at 200 °C for 8‑12 minutes until golden. Serve with dips, cheese, vegetable spreads, or use as mini‑sandwich bases.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen breadsticks in an airtight bag in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, bake within 24 hours. Do not leave baked sticks at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

chicken-thigh-grilled-without-sauce-skin.title: Chicken thigh, grilled without sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the dark meat from the upper part of a bird's leg. Grilled without sauce and with the skin on, it stays juicy and flavorful while developing a crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Grilling at high heat creates aromatic compounds that enhance taste.
The skin retains some fat, making the dish richer and protecting the meat from drying out.
Chicken thighs are a staple in many cuisines, from barbecue to Asian marinades.
When cooked properly, the skin becomes crunchy without burning.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function, DNA synthesis, and skin health.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The skin increases the calorie density; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Formation of carcinogens when over‑charred
items.content: Excessive charring can produce heterocyclic amines; avoid burning the meat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled chicken thigh can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, used in sandwiches, or added to pasta. The skin can be eaten if crispy, or removed according to preference.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consuming.

cookie-peanut-butter-with-chocolate.title: Cookie with Peanut Butter and Chocolate

content.title: About
content.content: Cookie with peanut butter and chocolate is a crunchy biscuit that incorporates creamy peanut butter and chunks of dark chocolate. It blends the sweetness of chocolate, the nutty aroma of peanut butter, and the satisfying texture of a baked cookie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as an alternative to nut pastes.
The chocolate used is typically dark (70 % cocoa), giving a slightly bitter taste and a boost of antioxidants.
The peanut‑butter‑and‑chocolate combo is a classic American flavor pairing popular in desserts and snacks.
Cookies are often finished with an extra layer of chocolate glaze to intensify the flavor.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 % protein, helping to support muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats in peanut butter contribute to heart‑healthy nutrition.

items.title: Contains magnesium and vitamin E
items.content: These micronutrients support nerve function and protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate is high in flavonoids, which may improve circulation.

items.title: Satisfies sweet cravings with less added sugar
items.content: The natural sweetness of peanut butter often reduces the need for extra sugar compared to regular chocolate cookies.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a strong allergen; individuals with a peanut allergy should avoid this product.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Peanut butter and chocolate make the cookie energy‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some versions may contain added sugar, which is important to consider for diabetes management.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oils are used, trans fats may be present, which are detrimental to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a standalone snack, crumble it into yogurt or ice cream, or use it as a layer in dessert cakes. It pairs well with milk, coffee, or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation.

egg-sandwich-on-croissant-with-bacon.title: Egg and Bacon Sandwich on Croissant

content.title: About
content.content: The egg and bacon sandwich on a croissant combines a buttery flaky croissant, crispy bacon, and a creamy egg filling. It is usually served warm, sometimes with cheese, herbs, or a sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The croissant originated in Austria but became a French icon.
Bacon is traditionally made from pork belly, though turkey and plant‑based versions exist.
Eggs in the sandwich are often poached or scrambled to keep a soft texture.
Egg‑and‑bacon sandwiches are a staple of breakfast menus worldwide, from American diners to European brunch spots.
The contrast of buttery pastry, salty bacon, and rich egg creates a highly satisfying flavor profile.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and bacon provide complete protein needed for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Both ingredients supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Bacon contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant iron.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Butter‑based croissant offers monounsaturated fats that can be part of a balanced diet in moderation.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Egg yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: High saturated fat and sodium
items.content: Bacon and buttery pastry can raise cholesterol and blood pressure if eaten frequently.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: The combination of croissant, bacon, and egg makes the sandwich energy‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs may contain salmonella; ensure eggs are fully cooked.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People with egg allergy should avoid this product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, sliced in half. It pairs well with lettuce, tomato, avocado, or a drizzle of hollandaise. For a lighter version, choose a whole‑grain croissant and lean turkey bacon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, refrigerate wrapped tightly for up to 24 hours. Croissants can be frozen for up to 2 months, and bacon for up to 1 month when sealed in airtight bags.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried with vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is a pure source of protein with virtually no fat or carbohydrates. When prepared as an omelet, scrambled, or fried with vegetables, it retains most nutrients and gains additional vitamins and minerals from the veggies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g.
Unlike the yolk, the white contains almost no cholesterol.
Heat makes the protein more digestible, but excessive cooking can denature some amino acids.
Combining the white with vegetables improves the bioavailability of certain vitamins, such as vitamin C from peppers.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Protein is essential for tissue growth and repair, supports muscle mass and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The lack of fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Source of riboflavin (vitamin B2)
items.content: Riboflavin participates in energy metabolism and supports skin and eye health.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium has antioxidant properties and supports immune function.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper, spinach, tomatoes and other vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin K, folate and potassium.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive browning can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

items.title: Lack of fat
items.content: Because the dish is virtually fat‑free, adding a source of healthy fat (oil, nuts) may be advisable for balanced nutrition.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whisk egg whites with a splash of water, add chopped vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper, onion) and cook in a non‑stick pan with a small amount of oil until set. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Fresh egg whites can be kept in the fridge for 1‑2 days or frozen in portioned bags for up to 3 months.

green-peas-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-.title: Green peas, fresh, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are the edible seeds of the pea plant (Pisum sativum). In this form they are fresh, cooked and have added fat, which makes them richer in calories and flavor. The peas have a mild sweet taste and a tender texture, suitable as a side dish or an ingredient in soups, stews and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 10,000 years.
Freshly cooked peas retain most of their B‑vitamins and vitamin C, which can degrade during long storage.
Adding fat (oil or butter) enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and improves taste.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and are often used as a meat alternative in vegetarian diets.
In many countries peas are featured in traditional dishes such as Irish colcannon or French petits pois à la française.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain thiamine, folate and vitamin B6, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help maintain healthy blood pressure, and the added fat can improve lipid profiles when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Added fat increases the calorie density; people watching their weight should control portion size.

items.title: Flatulence issues
items.content: People with the rare genetic condition of reduced alpha‑galactosidase activity may experience gas and discomfort after eating peas.

items.title: Potential contamination
items.content: Improper storage of fresh peas can lead to bacterial growth; use the product within a few days of preparation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be enjoyed on their own, tossed into salads, added to soups or stews, or used as a filling for pies. A light sprinkle of salt and a drizzle of olive oil or melted butter are recommended when serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze portions in a freezer‑safe bag; they retain flavor and nutrients for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Jambalaya is a classic Creole dish made with rice, meat (usually chicken, sausage, or pork), vegetables, and aromatic spices. The dish offers a rich, hearty flavor thanks to the combination of protein, carbohydrates, and veggie components.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Jambalaya originates from Louisiana, USA, and is considered the state’s signature dish.
Traditional recipes rely on the “Holy Trinity” of spices: paprika, thyme, and oregano.
There are two main styles: Creole (with tomatoes) and Cajun (without tomatoes).
It is cooked in a single pot, allowing all flavors to meld together.
Rice is added at the end so it absorbs the full depth of the broth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat component provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Spices and meat contribute B6 and niacin, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Paprika and other spices contain carotenoids and polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc, and magnesium, supporting immunity and muscle function.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using processed sausage or ready‑made sauces can make the dish very salty, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Meat, rice, and oil make jambalaya energy‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may react to paprika, chili, or mustard.

items.title: Food‑borne bacteria risk
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella or campylobacter contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve jambalaya hot, often with a lemon wedge, fresh herbs (parsley, green onion), and a side of crusty bread. Add hot sauce to taste if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 2 months and thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Snack cake, white is a small, individually wrapped portion of soft sponge cake topped with a light white cream. It is designed for a quick snack and is often sold in single‑serve packaging.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White snack cakes are frequently used as a base for dessert assortments and gift packs.
The cake batter typically contains eggs, sugar, vegetable oil, and a small amount of leavening agent.
The cream may be made from cream cheese, whipped cream, or mascarpone, sometimes flavored with vanilla or lemon zest.
The product is marketed as a convenient on‑the‑go snack.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat, delivering a quick boost of energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter and dairy in the cream supply a small amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs contribute B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, which support metabolism.

items.title: Milk and egg allergy
items.content: Contains dairy and eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet cream and cake make the product calorie‑dense; people monitoring sugar intake should limit consumption.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some versions may use partially hydrogenated oils; check the ingredient list if you have cardiovascular concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snack cake is ready to eat straight from the wrapper. It can be sliced and paired with coffee, ice cream, or fruit sauce. For a softer texture, gently warm the cream before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cakes in a cool, dry place, in their original packaging or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 5 days) keep them refrigerated to maintain cream freshness.
